translation:
_Guruki karni chit dhare, shikh sohi chandaal. Taki sangat parasram, nishche gase kaal._ (Parshuram says: whichever disciple keeps dwelling in his mind on the guru's conduct and finds fault with it is like an untouchable; keep company with such a person, and death will surely devour you.)

_Guru je avagun kare, shikh so dekhe naahi. Gyani jaane Ramroop, dubdha dilme naahi._ (Gyaniji Maharaj says: whatever fault the guru may commit, the disciple should not dwell on it in his mind; rather he should regard the guru as a form of Lord Ram himself, and hold no doubt or suspicion in his heart.)

_Ekah eva paro bandhur-vishame samupasthite, Gurusakaladharmatma, yatra-akinchanago Harih._ (Shridhar says of the guru: in a terrible calamity like death, the one true friend who comes to help is the guru alone. The guru is righteous in every way, for Shri Hari, who loves the poor and destitute, dwells within the guru's heart.)

_Yasya sakshad bhagavati tranadeepapade gurau, martyasaddhih shrutam tasya sarva kunjharashochavat. ||26||_ (The guru who lights the lamp of knowledge in the heart is God himself, present before us. If a foolish person regards him as merely human, then all the scripture that person has heard is as useless as an elephant's bath, which only covers it in dust again.)

**Sugar-Candy Food**

The parable of how faith was ruined by eating sweets from the hand of a sakut (a self-serving, worldly-minded person, as opposed to a true devotee).

Once, at a time of famine, a Smarta (worldly, self-interested) Brahmin, his Brahmin wife, and their son were travelling along and came to Shri Gokul. There, the parents deceived their seven-year-old boy and abandoned him on the bank of the river Yamuna, then went away. The child began to wail. Shri Gosainji happened to come to that spot. When he asked the child who he was, the boy said, "I am a Brahmin's child. My mother and father have left me and gone." Gokulnath Gosainji felt compassion. He had the boy's head shaved, gave him a mala and tilak, placed his hand upon his head, and named him Govardhan. He entrusted him with the seva of Shri Govardhannathji and put the keys of the storehouse in his hands. He instilled in him the spirit of a servant among the Vaishnavs, and the boy came to love the path of devotion to God very dearly.

Some days later, his parents returned to that same bank of the Yamuna at Gokul, to the very spot where they had abandoned him, and both of them heard the child. He was crying loudly, so the people of Braj living in Gokul came and told the Smarta Brahmin the news that his son's name had been made Govardhan, and that Shri Gosainji had entrusted him with the seva of Govardhannathji. Just then that Vaishnav boy came carrying a golden pot on a yoke to fetch water, and the people of Braj pointed him out to his parents. His mother and father broke down weeping, but he did not even look at his own parents. They stayed there like this for five days, grieving constantly, but the boy, being a Vaishnav bound by such strict vows, would not let even their shadow fall upon him. One day, at the bank of the Yamuna, his mother came and fell at his feet, since Govardhan Thakorji's water-carrier had come there to fill water. His father then tied up a lump of sugar-candy and gave it to him, saying, "Please take this sweet; let our anguish be relieved." Knowing their sorrow, the boy put the sugar-candy in his mouth twice, and as soon as it entered his mouth he said, "Now your wish is fulfilled" — and went on his way. But once that sweetness had gone down into his stomach, he said, "You are grieving for my sake; I will come with you." He made a promise to his mother and father, saying, "I will bring some wealth with me." Then he took all of Hari's ornaments — the diamonds, pearls, and jewels — locked up the temple, handed over the storeroom, took the keys with him, and set off with his parents. The three of them walked a distance of three, five, ten kos. Meanwhile, in Shri Gokul, all the Vaishnavs were crying out in great distress because a theft had occurred in the temple. They sent Vaishnavs out in all directions to search. At that time, Shri Gosainji said, "He will not go anywhere and leave the seva of Nathji's temple. His parents were self-serving, and he has taken sweets from their hand; that sweet will remain in his stomach, and only once it has passed through and its effect wears off will he come back. Since Shrinathji's chamber is locked, he is bound to return — that is what I say." After some time, when all the Vaishnavs were sitting together in assembly, that boy came in, weeping and wailing loudly. He told the whole story at length: "As long as the wicked portion of that sweet remained in my stomach, I was carried away by it, and once that unoffered, impure portion had passed through me, I became blind to the truth and could not see the way ahead. That is why, Maharaj, I have left that wickedness behind and have come to take refuge at your feet. I have brought back all the ornaments, the diamonds, pearls, and jewels." Saying this, he handed the keys to the guru and bowed at his feet, weeping loudly. Then Vyasji spoke this sakhi in that assembly —

_Vyas bohot meethai vipraki, taame lago ju aag. Shri Vrindavanke swapachke, rahiye sevak hoiye maag. ||1||_

_Vyas Vrindavanke swapachke, rahiye sevak hoi. Taathe bhinna na aaniye, peeje pagraj ghoi. ||2||_

(Hariram Vyasdasji says: however great a Brahmin may be, if his sweets — being the sweets of a non-Vaishnav — are bound to spoil, let them spoil; give them up. But one who dwells in Vrindavan-dham, the realm of devotion, even if he is of the lowest caste, a bhangi, is still to be preferred — become his servant and beg from him if need be. Vyasdasji says: one who dwells in Vrindavan, even a devotee of the bhangi caste, should be served; do not think of him as different or lesser — rather, wash his feet and drink that water, that is, welcome and honor him with the greatest respect.)

**The Crow that Perched on the Ship — A Parable of the Bond between Guru and Disciple**

Jivandasji said: Once there was a ship with its helmsman. While it was under way it anchored partway along its route. A crow then flew and settled upon it, and after a while the ship set sail again. The crow began flying about, looking in all four directions, and then came and settled right back on the ship. "Now tell me, of the two — the ship and the crow — which is the better?" Hearing this, none of the other Vaishnavs answered, so Vaishnav Jivandasji himself said: the nature of the ship is that of the guru, and the nature of the bird is that of the disciple. In this world one sees only the water of worldly craving; if there were somewhere else to go, one would go there, but where can one go in the water? That is why the crow keeps returning again and again to perch upon the ship.

_Sitapati Raghunathji, tum lagi meri daur. Jaise kaag jahajko, soojhat aur na thaur._ (In this doha it is said: O Sitapati Ram, my striving can carry me only so far as reaching your shelter, with whatever strength I have — just as a crow, clinging to the ropes of a ship, has nowhere else to go besides the ship, so too I find no refuge anywhere besides you. A person can exert only the strength that lies within his own capacity.)

_Kabir mere sahab aap ho, tum lagi meri daur. Jaise pankhi jahajka, aur na soojhe thaur._ (Kabir says: O my Lord, you alone are mine; my striving reaches only as far as you — just as the ship's bird finds no other refuge in sight besides the ship.)

_Kabir jal kaasht boodai nahi, kaha bhai kahaanki preet. Oopna seencha jaanke, eh badaanki reet. ||1||_ (Das Kabirji says: a log of wood does not sink in water — tell me, brother, what is the nature of this love? The answer: "I have watered and nurtured this wood, knowing it as my own," and it is out of that knowledge that one does not let it drown; such a noble sentiment belongs only to the great and elevated souls.)

_Pathar pabedo naakhtaan, kalpa vriksha phal det. Aise Harijan Jeevna, bhaage jaateku det. ||2||_ (Jivandasji Maharaj says: even when a loose stone is hurled at it, a wish-fulfilling tree still gives fruit in return; in the same way, the devotees of Hari shower their grace even upon those who trouble them and run away.)

_Kabir mein seenchyo het jaanke, o hoi neem kaath. Dekho gat sansaarki, sheesh par paadi baat._ (Das Kabirji says: "I have watered this, knowing it as my own" — even should it turn out to be bitter neem wood, that very wood, out of love, makes a path for the water over its own crown; such is the way love runs in this world — understand it well.)

_Poot pithaara baapko, gohan laaga jaay. Lobh mithai haath de, aapan gaya bhoolaay. Deenhi khaand padtikikar, man mein ros upaay. Rovat rovat mili gaya, pita piyaare jaay._ (Das Kabirji says: a son is dear to his father, to his guru; he keeps running along in his father's, his guru's, embrace. The devotee went for shelter to the Lord, to the guru; then the father put a sweet in the son's hand — the mistaken notion that the soul is meant for worldly enjoyment — and lured by greed for that sweet, the son let go of the guru's hand and forgot his own true self. But then he threw away the packet of sugar-candy, anger rose in his mind, and weeping, weeping, he went and was reunited with his beloved father, his guru. Once the devotee gave up the objects of the senses, he attained Hari.)

**Kundali**

_Gordhan gaando thai gayo, maat taatni khai khaand. Hakk vanu santjan khaayna, khaay te to jan bhaand. Khaay te to jan bhaand, khaataan jag haansi thashe. Kahun chun laai het, na samajya maaraj khaase. Trikam lakhe kritaghnanun kaand, samajaavva vichaar thayo. Maat taatni khaand khai, Gordhan gaando thai gayo._

(Trikamdas Govardhandas Suryodhoda writes: the Smarta Brahmin's son Gordhan lost his senses after eating sugar-candy from his parents' hand, and so committed theft in the temple and fled together with his parents. This is how true saints behave — they never accept anything beyond what rightfully belongs to them, and those who obtain and enjoy things in this improper way are nothing but clowns and buffoons. Anyone who indulges in this way will only bring shame and disgrace upon themselves before the world. I say this with pure love and affection; if you proceed without understanding it, you will only suffer for it. Trikamdas [says]: I am writing this account of the wretched state to which an ungrateful person, one who harms his own benefactor, is reduced. It occurred to me to explain this through the example of how the son Gordhan lost his senses after eating the sugar-candy given by his mother and father.)

**Kavit**

_Gordhan gaando thai gayo, sakut ni khai khaand. Maat pita hova chataan, mati thai gai ti bhaand. Mati thai gai ti bhaand, daagina laine naatho. Thaishna swami haandh, kaadhish nahi jaraay laantho. Thaish na swami haanth, kaadhish nahi jaraay laantho. Thai fare chhe sevak raand, sakut sang hadghoot thayo. Sakut ni khai khaand, Gordhan gaando thai gayo._

(Trikamdas Govardhandas Suryodhoda writes: because Gordhan ate the sugar-candy from the hand of his self-serving parents, his mind grew as corrupted as a clown's, even though his own real parents had given it to him — because they were sakut, his understanding, being fed on that food, turned as base as a buffoon's. His intelligence became as spoiled as a clown's, so he took the temple's ornaments and fled together with his parents. So, O worthy soul of high standing, do not become as proud and unruly as an overfed bull; nurturing such pride will bring you to nothing [text unclear/incomplete in the source at this point].)

As the Chandogya Upanishad, 7.26.2, says:

_Aahaarashuddhau sattvashuddhih, sattvashuddhau dhruva smritih. Smritishuddhau sarvagranthinaam vipramokshah._

(This is explained thus: when purity of food — that is, the purity of one's perceptions and understanding gained through it — is attained, purity of the inner faculties follows, and one gains the benefit of the quality of sattva. When the inner faculties are purified, steady remembrance is attained; through that, one is able to grasp true principles, and such discerning wisdom awakens. From the resulting attainment of true remembrance, all the knots of bondage are completely loosened, and the bondage of worldly existence is destroyed.)

On the theme "as the food, so the belch; as the water, so the speech," Trikamdas Govardhandas wrote Kundali No. 618 — Diary 2.32, page 200.

**Kundali**

_Anna tevo odkaar chhe, anna tevun man. Sakut anna khaava thaki, adham bane chhe jan. Adham bane chhe jan, khaand khaai Gordhan gaando. Sutradhaar samaaj, trirashi jaldi maando. Kahe Trikam sudharel jan, oont sam par upkaari chhe. Anna tevun mand, anna tevo odkaar._

(Trikamdas says: as the food one eats, so the belch of wind that follows; likewise, as the food one eats, so the mind becomes. By eating the food of a sakut, a person becomes base and sinful — as base as Gordhan's intelligence became corrupted after eating the sugar-candy of his self-serving parents. So, O saints and mahants who bear responsibility for guiding society, quickly work out the lesson from this example: even though this sakut's son was eventually redeemed, still, if eating a sakut's food could corrupt his intelligence, then the intelligence of people like us could just as easily be spoiled. Therefore, Trikamdas says, those who call themselves cultured and refined people often present themselves as being of the highest order, like a camel, claiming to do good to others, while remaining careless and indifferent toward the ordinary, lower classes, like a jackal — such people are hypocrites. So, whatever food you eat, that same corruption will enter your mind and intellect.)

_Deepo bhakshayate dhvaantam, kajjalam cha prasrayate. Yathaannam bhakshayet nityam, jaayate taadrshi prajaa._ (A lamp consumes darkness, and in doing so produces soot; likewise, whatever food a person eats every day, offspring of that same nature are born to them.)

_Kinchidvedamayam paatram, kinchit paatram tapomayam. Paatraanaam uttamam paatram, shoodraannam yasya nodare._ (Some vessel may be precious for being learned in the Vedas, some vessel may be radiant with austerity, but the best vessel of all is the one within whose stomach there is no food from the house of a base or unworthy person.)

_Avaishnavasya hastaannam divyadeshaadupaagatam. Hareh prasaadam teertham cha prayatne vivarjayet._ (Even if food from the hand of a non-Vaishnav has come from a divine and holy place, and is Hari's own prasad or holy water, one should nonetheless make every effort to avoid and give it up.)

_Mero man anatahi sachu paavai, jaise udat jahaajko pakshi, phiri jahaaj pai asai. Jo nar kamal nainko tajikai, aanadevko dhyaavai. Vidyamaan Gangaatat pyaaso, durmati koop banaavai. Jin madhukar antuj ras chaakhyo, taahi karil na bhaavai. Surdas prabhu Kaamdhenu taji, chheri kaun duhaavai._

(Surdasji says: my mind finds no true peace anywhere else. Just as the ship's crow flies out over the ocean and then comes back to settle on the ship again, so too my mind does not stray anywhere else. In the same way, a person who abandons the lotus-eyed Lord and worships other gods is like a foolish man who digs a well for himself while standing right at the bank of the Ganga, dying of thirst. One who has tasted the lotus's nectar as a bee will never find the castor-plant's flower pleasing. Surdas says: why, then, would anyone abandon the wish-fulfilling cow Kamdhenu to go milking a goat?)

In the diary from Samvat 1984 (the Adhadhiya notebook), pages 34–33, is written the following account by the revered Yadunath, dated Samvat 1984, Magsar Sud 4, Monday, 28-11-1927, and also on page 33, Magsar Sud 3, Sunday, 27-11-1927: "Today, some portion of the conversation that took place with Bhagat Garbadbhai Ramdas of Kandari, Taluka Karjan, is recorded below."

Originally, the first seat was not at Puniyad. A government official had once come to inspect the temple, at a time when the swami was away from the residence. When the official arrived and looked, it turned out that he had received his answer from the swami and gone away. On the strength of this, the seat upon which Ishwar, that is Jivanji Maharaj, had sat while manifesting the swami's form, came to be regarded as worthy of worship and was kept for veneration; the founding of the gaadi is counted from that time. Regarding the greatness of that seat, he related another account, as follows. Chhagan Krishnaram, a resident of Kandari, who was the moneylender — and also the friend — of Jagannath Swami: Garbadbhai says from his own experience that once, when they had gone there to settle a matter of money owed, and began to sit near a pillar at the fair, they were stopped and told, "Do not sit here," because that spot belonged to Bhai Jagannath Swami, as he was addressed by that name. Garbadbhai then asked, "Do you yourself not sit here either?" The reply was, "No" — meaning that the seat and bolster near the pillar where Jagannath Swami used to sit, no one else made use of.

He also told an account regarding food, as follows.

At the same Krishnaram's house, they had adopted Ambalal, the son of his sister-in-law, whose own father's ancestral home lay on the bank of the Narmada. On one occasion, provisions had come to Krishnaram, as a patron, for a feast for the Bhoi caste; on that occasion a Dandi Sanyasi also arrived and asked for food. Since the meal was to be served late, food was given to him quite late, and by then night had fallen. The sannyasi stayed there overnight and was given a blanket to sleep under. In the morning, his mind turned to covetousness over the blanket, and he took it and left. Further on, he had a change of heart over having taken it, and after going two or three kos, he repented and came back to return it; and when he inquired whose food he had eaten there, and reflected on how his austere discipline had been broken, he was overcome with remorse. This incident, it is said, occurred in the winter of Samvat 1983.

A similar incident had occurred that was reported in the Kalyan monthly magazine, and I have mentioned it in my discourse too. At the house of a certain sheth, a sadhu-mahatma had come as a guest. The sheth attended to him and fed him, then had him lie down to rest in his own office, while the sheth himself sat counting money. In the meantime, someone suddenly called for the sheth, so he left the money just as it was and went outside. The sadhu, his eyes turning covetous, picked up a bundle of ten thousand rupees and made off with it. The next day, when the sheth's money was found missing, the sadhu was struck with remorse, thinking, "I gave up my mother, I gave up my father, I gave up wife, son, and wealth — so why did my intention turn corrupt over this money?" Fearing that the sheth would beat all his servants over it, the sadhu returned; and indeed, the sheth was scolding all his servants at that time. The sadhu then said, "Sheth-ji, do not beat anyone — I am the one who took the money." The sheth said, "I never suspected you at all." The sadhu then asked, "Sheth-ji, what kind of grain did you feed me, that my mind turned so corrupt?" The sheth replied that sacks of rice used to come to his warehouse from a railway godown, and it was from that rice he had fed him. The sadhu then said, "It was from eating stolen food that my mind became corrupted."

The Muslim community, too, places great importance on honesty (iman). Regarding the ascetic Ahmad Harsh, it is written in Kalyan magazine, Year 7, Issue 9, page 1165, Registration No. 18, as follows: One day his mother cooked food and brought it to him, saying, "Son, this food has been cooked from the grain of our own house, so eat it without any hesitation." Ahmad said, "No — one day I saw that our neighbor's grain was also mixed into ours. This neighbor gathers his wealth unjustly. Since his grain is mixed into ours, I feel great reluctance about eating this food."

Muslims do not believe in alcohol or gambling. That is why, in America, stores owned by Muslims do not sell liquor or lottery tickets — whether or not they themselves drink, they do not engage in the business of selling liquor.

It is written in Hand-written Manuscript No. 330, page 146, that devotees once asked Jivanji Maharaj whether God truly partakes of the offering placed before the garlanded image or not. Jivanji Maharaj said he would tell them at some point. Once, Vaishnavs had brought thals of prasad; all the plates were gathered together except one devotee's plate, which was kept separate. Then a garland was offered upon that separately-kept plate, and at that moment a bead of the garland burst. From this Jivanji Maharaj explained that this particular plate had been prepared with someone else's, unearned money, and that was why the bead had burst — thereby proving that God does indeed partake of the offered plate. In that manuscript, the account is recorded in the old dialect of the time, to this same effect: the devotees asked Jivanji whether the Lord truly eats the offered food; Jivanji told them he would explain. All the Vaishnavs were asked to bring their plates; all were gathered together except one Vaishnav's plate, which was kept apart because it had been made with someone else's money. When the garland was placed upon it, its bead burst — and from this everyone understood that the Lord does not accept anything not rightfully earned; and by this sign, everyone came to know that God does indeed partake of what is offered.

_Saat paanch sangi mile, surabhi bhadai uthaay. Jeevan man atakyo Shaamsun, sau neek na it ut jaay._ (Jivandasji Maharaj says: seven or five saintly companions come together and lift this wish-fulfilling cow of loving devotion up out of the mire of worldly delusion. With such a spirit, Jivandasji says, my mind has become so firmly fixed and absorbed in loving devotion to Lord Krishna that it does not stray even a little from it.)

There is also an episode recorded among the miracles of Jivanji Maharaj: a certain woman once invited Jivanji Maharaj for a meal. But when he sat down to take the prasad, Jivanji Maharaj remained seated without having offered the garland first. When everyone asked him the reason, Jivanji Maharaj said that this prasad was already impure, because the woman had cooked it using fire carried hand to hand directly from her neighbor's house. In this way, one must maintain the utmost caution and keep no dealings whatsoever with a sakut in matters concerning food and prasad.

There is the example of Upamanyu, or of Shvetaketu, who agreed to eat another's leftover food in order to have a violent sacrifice performed.

(From the Pranavidhi text, pages 16–17:) Whatever a person eats or drinks — whatever substances, creatures, or people come into contact with him — and finally, whatever thoughts he keeps his mind absorbed in, the nature of his life-force is shaped as a result of all these. From every object, whether inert or living, whoever remains close to it keeps absorbing the effect of its subtle influence; that is to say, one who stays near any given object cannot help but absorb the effect of that object's subtle influence. Clothes once worn, water once drunk, food once eaten, a book once touched — all of these become imbued with the subtle influence of the one who wore, drank, ate, or touched them, and before enough time has passed for that influence to fade, if someone else then uses that same item, this hidden quality absorbed into it is transferred to the new user. It is with all of this in mind that such rules have come into practice: not to drink water someone else has already drunk from, not to eat food someone else has already eaten from, not to eat from the same vessel as another, not to wear clothes someone else has worn, and rules about what may or may not be touched, and what may or may not be eaten. Bronze absorbs such subtle influence more quickly than copper or brass and does not release it again for a longer time; that is precisely why it is regarded as a metal that becomes unusable if touched by a person of another caste.

In Samvat year 1709, on Vaishakh Sud 5, Haribhai came from village Mauj Aritha to Shahapura. He took Vaishnav Jivandasji along and went himself to the fields; all the other Vaishnavs went along into the field as well. There they saw abundant rasal (sugarcane produce). Haribhai then said, "Vaishnavji, how is there such rasal in this month of Vaishakh?" Vaishnav Jivandasji answered by quoting the twenty-first saying of Bhakta Biradavali, of Bajid (Hand-written manuscript No. 5, page 242):

_Dharti ambar aadya dei, ravi shashi paani pavan. Sant jaan e to rachyo, nahitar kaaran kavan. ||1||_ (Having first given the earth and sky, and then the sun, moon, water, and wind — know that all this was created for the sake of the saints, for what other reason would it have been made?)

In the world, God first created the five great elements — earth, sky, and so on — and likewise created the sun, moon, water, and wind, knowing that the saints and devotees are all his servants; he made all these creations for their good. Otherwise, God says, what need would there have been for him to create all of this?

Jivanji Maharaj also says the same:

_Main sabras keeno Jeevna, so apne janke kaaj. To peechhe joolan leeno, tab paayo naam Brijraaj. ||32|| Das._

(Jivandasji Maharaj says: I have prepared every kind of flavorful dish, and I did it for the sake of my own devotees; and it was only after taking the portion left over from their eating that I attained the name Brijraj, Lord of Braj.)

Then, sitting beneath a mahuda tree, he spoke a parable: just as the one who operates the water-wheel at a well causes the water of the well's grace to flow, and makes channels to water the sugarcane — yet weeds and wild grasses also spring up in those very channels — so is this entire universe merely such a field. The devotees of Hari are the sugarcane; the self-serving, like a forest of weeds, have grown thick and overgrown. That is why the sugarcane saplings grow only slowly, little by little. On this, he gave this sakhi —

_Ek palakmein sab kiya, trilok ekvees brahmaand. Harijan kartaan Jeevna, laage din dashvees._ (Jivandasji Maharaj says: the all-powerful Lord created the entire three worlds and the twenty-one universes in a single blink of an eye. But, mighty as he is, it takes him ten to twenty days to make a single devotee.)

(Tri.Go. Diary 2032, page 81:)

**Kundali**

_Ek palakmein sab kiya, lok ekvees brahmaand. Harijan kartaan Jeevna, laage din dash vees. Laage din vees, patitne punit kartaan. Sahejmein sudhare nahi, prayatna karine martaan. Kahai Trikam padho addaavees kon kon kaho, tar gaya. Trilok brahmaand ekvees brahmaand, ek palakmein sab kiya._

(Jivandasji Maharaj says: the all-powerful Lord created the three worlds and the twenty-one universes in a single blink of an eye. Yet, mighty as he is, it takes him ten to twenty days to make a devotee; it takes ten to twenty days to purify a sinner. A sinner does not reform easily; one must labor at it even to the point of exhausting oneself. Trikamdas says: read Adhyaruji's twenty-eight kirtans, and see for yourself who among the saintly and the base was redeemed first — "_Kaashta klevar vipla niramla kidha neer, adhan enipar osharyaa pachhi sant sharir_" [unclear, an archaic quoted line — roughly: the impure body, made pure by water, gives way; only after such lowliness is refined does the body of a saint follow]. Thus, though the three worlds and the twenty-one universes could be made in a single instant, the making of a saint takes a very long time.)

In this episode with Haribhai, Jivanji Maharaj gave a glimpse of his own way of life. Whomever he placed his hand upon — that is, whomever he made his follower — he never held out his own hand beneath that person's hand, meaning he never accepted anything from him; instead, he supported himself through his own farming. That understanding comes through here. Haridas Nadiadao, referring to this matter, wrote in the Bhaktamal: "_Jeeva ja shir kar dharyo, ta kar tar odyo nahi_" — meaning that whomever Jivanji Maharaj placed his hand upon and accepted as his own, he never stretched out his own hand beneath that person's hand to take anything from him. It was when Haribhai came here from Aritha that Jivandasji Maharaj sat with him beneath the mahuda tree in his own field where the mahuda trees grew, and they had this conversation there. Speaking with reference to farming, Jivanji Maharaj said that God made things like the five great elements — earth, water, air, fire, and sky — for the sake of his devotees; but just as a farmer works the water-wheel to bring water for his sugarcane, weeds and other grasses also spring up along the channel. From this example, it is implied that the self-serving too are nourished by the merit of true devotees. Hence he said —

_Gau santanke kaaran, Hari varsaavat meh. Taake peechhe Parasuram, duniya paale deh. ||1|| Gau sant bhookhe mare, duniya lap lap khaay. Parasa taa paap the, sooka pad pad jaay. ||2||_

(Parashuram says: for the sake of the cow and the saints, God sends down the rain, and behind them, all the people of this world are nourished and sustain their bodies. Meanwhile the poor cows and saints go hungry, while the people of the world eat their fill greedily; because of this sin, famine keeps falling upon the land, again and again.)

_Uge tahaan vaave nahi, aur vaave tahaan jal jaay. Tulsi aa sansaarmein, maal mashkara khaay._

(Where it would grow, no one plants it; and where it is planted, the water simply drains away — so, Tulsi says, in this world it is the wicked and the mocking who reap the wealth. This means: if sound teaching is given to a worthy person, it bears real fruit; but if, without discernment, one waters the seed of teaching upon the unworthy, then whatever benefit results will only be enjoyed by rogues and cheats, while good people gain nothing from it.)

God produced costly things like dried fruits, cashews, and almonds in Kabul, while in Vrindavan he grew only thorny clusters of wild ker. Yet even a humble thing, appearing in the right place, can prove to be of good use.

_Kabir kahaa kahun us Raamko, mile to deun shikh. Nigura maanas raaj kare, Harijan maage bheekh._

(Das Kabirji says: what shall I say about this Ram, how strange he is; if I could only meet him I would give him a piece of my mind — asking why such an unfair arrangement exists, that people with no guru, far removed from devotion, live in comfort and rule, while your own devotees, poor souls, suffer hardship and go begging.)

_Kabir Harijanku main raaj gau, to sab Harijan ho jaaye. Narak kund khaali padai, Vaikunthmein na samaaye._

(Das Kabirji himself answers: if I were to give power and sovereignty to my devotees, then everyone would become a devotee, following their example — and then the pits of hell would stand empty, while heaven would overflow, unable to hold everyone.)

_Sabka daata Ram hai, raaja parja bheradaa. Uparse paani na pare, to kaun kisiku det._

(God is the giver of all — be it king or ordinary subject, whatever form they take. But if rain does not fall from above, then neither king nor subject would be able to give anything to anyone.)

_Mani maanek moghe kiye, songha taran jal anaaj. Tulsi taathe jaaniye, Ram bade garib nivaaj._

(Tulsidas says: God made precious stones like jewels and rubies costly, while making grass, water, and grain cheap and abundant — such is the plan of creation. From this, know that Lord Ram is a great benefactor and friend of the poor.)

In Hand-written Manuscript No. 98, page 29, there is an account of how the rasayan (the produce, that is, the watermelon) grew lush and green in Shahapura: it uses the parable of a man who makes a garden by irrigating it with water from a well, in which grasses and other things also grow, and explains the point in a kind of mystical, parable-language — the one who draws the water from the well is the Compassionate Lord, the young plant is the saint, and the weeds and wild grasses are the world; God made this rasayan for the sake of the saints. In this Manuscript No. 98, the account of how God made this rasayan for the saints is written as follows —

"Ram Kabir Question," the second: In the village of watermelons, Shahapura, Vaishnav Jivandasji resides. In Samvat 1709, in Vaishakh, from Sud to Vad, Vaishnav Haribhai came from the village of Aritha and visited the garden and field there. There the Vaishnavs brought and offered the rasayan, Tarbuch Maharaj (the watermelon). "In the month of Chaitra, how did this rasayan come about?" — so the Vaishnav asked, and Vaishnavji answered, saying: "There is a certain well. From that well, he made a garden. There the saplings grow, and countless weeds and wild grasses are also nourished within it. The well-drawer's attention is on the saplings, though the weeds within also get nourished. This is a parable; the principle to understand is this: the well-drawer is the Compassionate Lord, the sapling is the saint, and the weeds and wild grasses are the world. This rasayan was made for the sake of the saints." This is the testimony of Parashuramji. Sakhi —

_Gau santanke kaarane, Hari varsaavat meh. Taake peechhe Farasuraam, duniya paale deh. ||1|| Gau santan bhookhe mare, duniya lap lap khaay. Taa kaaran the Farasuraam, sooka pad pad jaay. ||2||_ (The same meaning as before: for the sake of the cow and the saint, God sends rain, and through them the world is fed, while the cow and the saints go hungry as the world eats greedily; because of this sin, famine keeps recurring.)

The saying of Bhagat Biradavali: _Dharti ambar aad dai, ravi shashi paani pavan. Sant jaan eno racho, nahi to kaaran kavan. ||3||_ (Having first given the earth and sky, then the sun, moon, water and wind — know that all this was created for the sake of the saints; otherwise what reason would there be for it?)

_Main janki nidhi, jan nidhi meri. Main janki nidhi, jan nidhi meri. Main so mamjan, mamjan so main. Sun Kamla saachi so teri. ||tek|| Sindhu suta bilag jin maano. Toon jan te kachhu naahi ghaneri. Ashta siddhi nav nindaa chatur mugat, so mere bhagatanki cheri. ||1|| Main saakaar bhayo janke hit, Brahma paar na paave heri. Main ek paav gadho kar jori, bhakta aadheen deen vrat leri. ||2|| Teen lok aur bhuvan chatur das, bhakta vatsal mero birad aheri. Sukh saagar senike saaiyaan, bhagatanke vash Ved kaheri. ||3||_

(God says: I am the treasure of my devotees, and my devotees are my treasure. I am my devotees' own self, and my devotees are my own self. Listen, Kamala, I speak this truth to you, and you must accept it as true: O daughter of the ocean, never think of my devotee as separate from me; you yourself are no greater than my devotee. The eight siddhis, the nine nidhis, and the four kinds of liberation are but handmaidens of my devotee. I took on a form with attributes for the sake of my devotees — a mystery even Brahma cannot fathom. I stand ready, on one foot, hands joined, submissive before my devotee, bound by a humble vow. In the three worlds and the fourteen realms, it is my very nature to hold deep affection for my devotees. I am the ocean of happiness, the Lord of all, and, as the Vedas themselves declare, I remain under the control of my devotees.)

Having written the above, it is further stated in Manuscript No. 98, page 31, that this Prashna (question) of the Samagam belongs to Vaishnav Jivandasji, as recorded in the register kept in the Parthara of Dalidas Vala, of Vayda Pol; it has been copied from what Vaishnav Sitaram wrote out in full at Agra, in Samvat 1796, Magha Sud. If any letters appear faint or unclear, please read them with correction as needed.

_Sadguru sandesa mokala, kachaabachaa sab aap. Naam chintaaman Jeevna, je bhaave so paave. ||1|| Been asthaan kul kaachli, drishti pokhe parvaar. Hari janki sevak roodaan, kriyaa kataaksh aadhaar. ||2|| Nirgun re kaahaan pekhiye, lai chakh hridayaa vichaar._

(Jivandasji Maharaj says: the Sadguru sent word inviting everyone, young and old, small and great, to come to him, saying that his Name is like the wish-fulfilling jewel Chintamani; whoever desires anything of it, receives it. So take from that jewel-like Name whatever peace and joy you seek. Napaji Bhagat, in his chopai, says that just as a tortoise's young are nourished purely by the glance of the mother's compassionate gaze, without any touch, so too God is like that mother, and his devotees are like young ones sustained by his compassionate gaze; his devotees, his good servants, rely on the support of his glance and grace. Why, then, should one go looking elsewhere for the Formless? — O Lord, you yourself, through the eyes of your gracious gaze, hold and contemplate us within your own heart.)

Considering what is written above, in Hand-written Manuscript No. 98, pages 29 to 31, it can be understood that when Haribhai came from Aritha to Shahapura, it must have been in the hot season, around the month of Vaishakh, and he must have brought watermelons for the devotees to eat, watermelons he had grown in his own field named Vadiya. That field is presently Survey No. 201, measuring 5 vighas, 8 vasa, 3 acres, and 7 guntha, and is now in the possession of Bhagat Gunvantbhai, alias Jashbhai Vitthalbhai, of Baroda.
